title: Embeddings Simply Explained
description: What embeddings are, why they are foundational to modern AI, and how they make semantic search feel like magic.

data.text: How does a search engine know that "car" and "automobile" are the same thing? Or that "happy" and "joyful" are more similar than "happy" and "sad"? The answer is embeddings — the technology that gives AI a mathematical representation of meaning.
What is an embedding?

An embedding is a list of hundreds or thousands of numbers (a vector) that represents the meaning of a piece of text. The remarkable property: texts with similar meanings will have similar (mathematically close) vectors. This converts meaning into arithmetic.

data.title: The map analogy
data.text: Imagine placing every word on a giant map. Words with similar meanings cluster near each other. "King" is near "queen" and "monarch". "Happy" is near "joyful" but far from "sad". "Car" clusters with "vehicle", "automobile", "truck". An embedding is the precise coordinate of a piece of text on this meaning map.

data.caption: Embeddings place words with similar meanings close together in "vector space" — enabling semantic search

data.text: From words to numbers: how embedding models work

An embedding model is a neural network trained to read text and output a fixed-length list of numbers. The model is trained on enormous amounts of text, learning to place words and phrases that appear in similar contexts close together in vector space. This is not hand-coded — the model discovers the geometry of meaning purely from observing how words are used alongside each other.

Modern embedding models process more than single words. Sentence embedding models (like OpenAI's text-embedding-3 or Sentence-BERT) encode entire paragraphs as a single vector, capturing the overall meaning of a passage rather than individual word meanings. This is what makes them useful for document retrieval — you can embed a 500-word article into one vector and compare it directly against a query vector.

data.caption: How an embedding model converts text into a vector — the same process runs on both the query and all stored documents
data.definition:
flowchart TD
  A["Input text\n'affordable car'"] --> B[Tokeniser]
  B --> C[Transformer layers]
  C --> D[Pooling layer]
  D --> E["Output vector\n[0.23, -0.87, 0.45, 0.12, ...\n1536 numbers]"]  
  style A fill:#f0f0f0
  style E fill:#ddf4ff

data.text: Vector arithmetic: meaning as math

One of the most striking properties of embeddings is that relationships between meanings become relationships between vectors — and you can do arithmetic on them. The classic demonstration, discovered in early word embedding research, is: king − man + woman ≈ queen. The vector for 'king' minus the vector for 'man' plus the vector for 'woman' produces a vector very close to 'queen'. The model has encoded the concept of gender as a consistent direction in vector space.

data.caption: Vector arithmetic on embeddings — relationships between concepts become directions in space
data.definition:
graph TD
  A["king vector"] -->|"− man vector"| B["king − man"]
  B -->|"+ woman vector"| C["king − man + woman"]
  C -->|"≈ nearest neighbour"| D["queen vector"]
  style D fill:#d1f3d8,stroke:#1a7f37

data.text: This arithmetic works for many analogies: Paris − France + Italy ≈ Rome; doctor − man + woman ≈ nurse (though this also reveals how embeddings encode societal biases present in training data). The geometric structure of the vector space reflects the semantic structure of language — a remarkable emergent property that was not explicitly programmed.
Measuring similarity between vectors

Once text is converted to vectors, similarity is a mathematical calculation. The most common method is cosine similarity — it measures the angle between two vectors. Vectors pointing in nearly the same direction (small angle) have high similarity scores close to 1.0; vectors pointing in opposite directions have scores close to -1.0.

rows: Most semantic search systems; robust to vector length differences
Fast approximate search; used when vectors are normalised
Some clustering algorithms; less common in NLP

data.title: Cosine similarity in practice
data.text: A cosine similarity of 0.95 between two sentences means they are almost semantically identical. A score of 0.7–0.85 typically indicates strong topical relevance. Below 0.5, documents are generally on different topics. These thresholds vary by embedding model, so always calibrate against examples from your own domain.
How embeddings power semantic search
Traditional keyword search requires exact word matches. Semantic search uses embeddings to find content that means the same thing — even if it uses different words.

data.title: Keyword search vs semantic search
data.content:
Keyword search for "affordable car":
→ Only finds documents containing exactly "affordable" AND "car"
→ Misses: "budget vehicle", "cheap automobile", "low-cost transportation"

Semantic search for "affordable car":
→ Converts "affordable car" to its embedding vector
→ Finds all documents whose meaning-vector is close
→ Returns "budget vehicles", "cheap automobiles", "economical transport" — because their vectors are similar

This is why Perplexity can find relevant results even when you ask in your own words.

data.caption: Keyword search vs semantic search — the same query, dramatically different results

data.text: Embedding dimensions: how many numbers?

The number of dimensions in an embedding vector (e.g., 768, 1536, 3072) determines how much semantic information it can encode. Higher dimensions can represent finer-grained distinctions in meaning, but cost more to store and compare. Choosing the right dimensionality is a tradeoff between accuracy and performance.

rows: Good quality/cost balance for most applications
Higher accuracy; use when retrieval precision matters most
Strong performance on English retrieval tasks
Fast and lightweight; runs locally; good for low-resource environments
Strong performance on code and technical documents

data.text: Why embeddings matter for everyday AI users

items: Semantic search — searching your documents by meaning instead of exact keywords (Notion AI, Obsidian AI)
RAG systems — finding the right document to feed to an AI before it answers your question
Recommendations — finding similar items without rule-based matching (Netflix, Spotify both use this)
Duplicate detection — identifying near-identical content even with different wording
Classification — grouping similar documents or feedback automatically

data.text: Where embeddings appear in products you already use

rows: Songs are embedded into a vector space based on audio features and listening context; similar songs cluster together; your taste profile is a vector that is matched against song vectors
Incoming emails are embedded; the model finds semantically appropriate short reply suggestions from a pre-computed set
Your workspace pages are embedded at indexing time; when you search, your query is embedded and matched against page vectors — returning relevant pages even with different wording
FAQ answers are embedded; incoming customer messages are matched against the FAQ vector store; closest match is returned or fed to an LLM for a grounded answer
Job descriptions and candidate profiles are embedded; similarity matching surfaces relevant postings without requiring exact keyword overlap
Code in your open files is embedded; semantically relevant code snippets are retrieved and added to the model's context before generating suggestions

data.text: Vector databases: the engine behind RAG

A vector database stores embeddings and lets you find the most similar ones instantly — even across millions of documents. When you ask Perplexity a question or chat with a company's AI support bot, a vector database is doing the retrieval step behind the scenes.

data.caption: How embeddings power RAG: your question is converted to a vector, matched against stored document vectors, and the closest matches are sent to the AI
data.definition:
sequenceDiagram
  participant U as User
  participant EM as Embedding Model
  participant VDB as Vector Database
  participant LLM as Language Model

  U->>EM: "What is our refund policy?"
  EM->>VDB: [0.23, -0.87, 0.45, ...] (query vector)
  VDB->>LLM: Top 3 most similar document chunks
  Note over VDB,LLM: Documents whose vectors are
closest to the query vector
  LLM->>U: Answer grounded in actual policy docs

data.text: A traditional relational database (like PostgreSQL or MySQL) searches by exact value — you can find all rows where name = 'Alice' or price < 100. It cannot answer 'find me the 10 documents most semantically similar to this query.' Vector databases are purpose-built for this nearest-neighbour search problem, using index structures like HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) or IVF (Inverted File Index) to make similarity search across millions of vectors fast enough to use in real time.
Chunking: how documents are prepared for embedding

You cannot embed a 200-page document as a single vector and expect useful retrieval — the vector would average out too much meaning. Instead, documents are split into smaller chunks before embedding. Each chunk gets its own vector, and the vector database stores all of them. When a query arrives, the system retrieves the most relevant chunks — not the most relevant whole documents.

data.caption: Document chunking pipeline — each chunk is embedded independently and stored in the vector database
data.definition:
flowchart TD
  A[Long document\n200 pages] --> B[Chunker]
  B --> C1[Chunk 1\n~300 words]
  B --> C2[Chunk 2\n~300 words]
  B --> C3[Chunk 3\n~300 words]
  B --> CN[Chunk N\n~300 words]
  C1 --> E[Embedding model]
  C2 --> E
  C3 --> E
  CN --> E
  E --> VDB[Vector database]
  style A fill:#f0f0f0
  style VDB fill:#ddf4ff

data.text: Chunk size is a practical tuning decision. Smaller chunks (100–200 words) give more precise retrieval but may lose context — a sentence extracted from the middle of an argument may not make sense alone. Larger chunks (400–600 words) preserve more context but the vector averages more meaning, making retrieval less precise. Most production systems use chunks of 200–400 words with a small overlap between adjacent chunks to prevent information from being severed at chunk boundaries.
A note on bias in embeddings

Because embedding models learn from human-generated text, they absorb the biases present in that text. The classic example: in early word embedding models, the vector for 'doctor' was closer to 'man' than 'woman', reflecting historical biases in the training corpus. Modern embedding models apply debiasing techniques during training, but no model is fully free of this issue. For high-stakes applications — hiring, lending, content moderation — it is important to audit embedding-based systems for demographic bias before deployment.
Multilingual embeddings

Multilingual embedding models encode text from different languages into the same vector space. This means a query in English can retrieve a relevant document written in French, Spanish, or Japanese — without any translation step. The model learns that 'dog', 'chien', 'perro', and '犬' all cluster near each other because they appear in similar cross-lingual contexts during training.

Examples include OpenAI's text-embedding-3-large (strong multilingual performance), Cohere's embed-multilingual-v3.0, and the open-source paraphrase-multilingual-MiniLM-L12-v2. Multilingual embeddings are especially valuable for global products that need to search across documents in many languages from a single query interface.

data.title: Embeddings: the key ideas
points: Embeddings convert meaning into numbers (vectors) — similar meaning = similar vectors
They enable semantic search: find content by meaning, not just exact keywords
Vector databases store and search millions of embeddings instantly
RAG, recommendations, duplicate detection, and semantic search all run on embeddings
You use embeddings every time Perplexity finds relevant pages for your question
Documents must be chunked before embedding — chunk size is a key quality tuning lever
Multilingual embedding models can retrieve across languages from a single query
Embeddings inherit biases from their training data — audit before using in high-stakes decisions
